slide_title: Analysis of Seasonal Disease Patterns Using Government Health Data
purpose: Establish academic credentials and project context
on_slide_content: Project: Analysis of Seasonal Disease Patterns Using Government Health Data | Candidate: Khan Umar (B.Sc. Data Science, Sem III) | Institution: RP Institute, University of Mumbai | Surveillance Source: NCDC / IDSP Weekly Outbreak Reports | Geography: Maharashtra (36 Districts) | Baseline: 2022-2025 (539 Records, 21,955 Cases, 266 Deaths) | Comparison: 2026 W01-W32 (45 Records)
speaker_message: Good morning respected examiners. This presentation details an end-to-end data science investigation into seasonal outbreak patterns across Maharashtra using official NCDC/IDSP government health surveillance data from 2022 through 2026.

purpose: Justify why public health surveillance data requires data science methods
on_slide_content: Public Health Need: Pre-positioning medical supplies, diagnostic kits, and vector squads requires empirical seasonal timing | Surveillance Reality: Secondary administrative data contains reporting lag, variable thresholds, and extreme institutional outliers | Data Science Role: Transform raw administrative PDFs into auditable, statistically defensible seasonal intelligence without invalid causal claims
key_visual: Flow Diagram: Public Health Planning vs Administrative Surveillance Noise
speaker_message: Public health resource allocation relies on anticipating outbreak peaks. However, administrative outbreak notifications are frequently noisy and distorted by extreme events. Our role as data scientists is to extract robust seasonal signals while maintaining methodological boundaries.

purpose: State the core questions guiding the investigation
on_slide_content: Q1 (Seasonality): Do reported infectious disease outbreaks in Maharashtra follow statistically significant calendar-month concentrations? | Q2 (Stability): Are documented peak timing windows stable across years, or do they shift erratically? | Q3 (Spatial Concentration): Are seasonal patterns statewide or driven by localized district clusters? | Q4 (Data Artifacts): How do extreme outlier events distort case distributions relative to outbreak event frequencies?
key_visual: Analytical Framing Graphic: 4 Core Questions Matrix
speaker_message: We framed our inquiry around four precise questions: Are outbreak concentrations statistically seasonal? Are they inter-annually stable? Are they geographically uniform? And how do extreme institutional clusters distort our metrics?

purpose: Outline the formal project objectives (OBJ-01 to OBJ-08)
on_slide_content: OBJ-01: Reconstruct & validate clean secondary dataset from NCDC weekly reports | OBJ-02: Analyze monthly/annual distributions (2022-2025 baseline) | OBJ-03: Quantify concentration using CV, CR3, Entropy, Gini | OBJ-04: Evaluate seasonal peak windows & Kendall's W stability | OBJ-05: Examine district-level concentration & spatial focalization | OBJ-06: Assess outlier sensitivity & event-case divergence | OBJ-07: Conduct out-of-sample comparison with 2026 W01-W32 | OBJ-08: Formulate evidence-based public health surveillance implications
key_visual: Objectives Alignment Table (8 Objectives mapped to analytical phases)
speaker_message: Our work is structured across eight formal academic objectives spanning data engineering, exploratory analysis, non-parametric hypothesis testing, spatial auditing, sensitivity analysis, and out-of-sample validation.

purpose: Establish apex government data origin and integrity
on_slide_content: Primary Source: National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC), DGHS, Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Govt. of India | Programme: Integrated Disease Surveillance Programme (IDSP) Weekly Outbreaks | Publication Format: Official public PDF outbreak bulletins | Data Granularity: Weekly district-level outbreak notifications | Verified Fields: State, District, Disease, Cases, Deaths, Date of Start, Reporting Week, Current Status
key_visual: NCDC/IDSP Official Portal Architecture & Bulletin Sample
speaker_message: Our data originates exclusively from the official weekly outbreak reports of the NCDC/IDSP, the apex public health surveillance body of India, ensuring 100% official provenance without reliance on scraped or unverified third-party aggregators.

purpose: Define the precise analytical boundaries of the dataset
on_slide_content: Total Curated Dataset: 809 records across Maharashtra | Baseline Study Period: 2022-2025 (4 completed calendar years; 539 primary records) | Out-of-Sample Period: 2026 W01-W32 (45 primary records) | Cumulative Baseline Reported Cases: 21,955 across 5 primary families | Cumulative Baseline Reported Deaths: 266 | Geographic Scope: 36 Districts of Maharashtra | Missing Archive Periods: 2023 Weeks 15, 51, 52 (unpublished in public NCDC archive)
key_visual: Coverage Summary Card: 809 Total Records | 539 Baseline | 45 2026 YTD | 36 Districts
speaker_message: The authoritative analytical dataset comprises 809 total records from Maharashtra. The primary baseline spans four completed calendar years (2022-2025) with 539 primary family records, capturing 21,955 reported cases and 266 deaths. 2026 is strictly reserved as an out-of-sample comparison.

purpose: Demonstrate rigorous technical workflow from PDF to clean CSV
on_slide_content: Step 1: Automated PDF Acquisition & Archival Storage | Step 2: Tabular Extraction of Maharashtra Outbreak Sections into Structured JSON | Step 3: All analytical records programmatically linked to source PDF/page provenance, supported by targeted manual verification and global integrity checks | Step 4: Additive Analytical Standardization (ISO Weeks, Calendar Months, District Aliases) | Step 5: Dual Verification: Zero modification of raw disease text (disease_raw preserved) | Output: NCDC_Maharashtra_CLEAN_ANALYTICAL.csv (809 rows)
key_visual: Pipeline Flowchart: Acquisition -> Extraction -> Validation -> Standardization -> Frozen Master
speaker_message: Our data engineering pipeline enforced strict auditability. Records were programmatically linked to PDF page provenance, with targeted manual verification and global integrity checks. Analytical fields were added additively without overwriting raw strings.

purpose: Explain how raw source strings were mapped into 5 primary families
on_slide_content: Taxonomic Screening: 116 raw source strings -> 56 cleaned analytical labels -> 30 disease families -> 5 primary study families | Resolution: Standardized spelling variants ('Dengue?'), lexical forms ('ADD' vs 'Acute Diarrhoeal Disease'), and administrative prefixes | Primary Cohort Screening Criteria: (1) >= 40 baseline records, (2) present in >= 3 baseline years, (3) public health surveillance priority | Five Primary Study Families: Dengue (N=204), ADD (N=153), Malaria (N=70), Food Poisoning (N=69), Chikungunya (N=43)
key_visual: Taxonomy Flow: 116 Raw Strings -> 56 Cleaned Labels -> 30 Families -> 5 Primary Families
speaker_message: An essential data science step was resolving 116 raw source strings into 56 cleaned analytical labels, then 30 standardized families. Applying objective inclusion thresholds from Phase 5A yielded our five primary study cohorts, representing 92.5% of all baseline outbreak records in Maharashtra.

purpose: Define mathematical metrics used to evaluate seasonal patterns
on_slide_content: 1. Seasonal Index (Sm): Sm = 100 * (Mean_Monthly_Events / Annual_Mean_Monthly_Events); Sm > 100 indicates seasonal elevation | 2. Top-3 Concentration Ratio (CR3): Cumulative event percentage in top 3 calendar months | 3. Coefficient of Variation (CV): Relative dispersion across 12 months (sigma / mu) | 4. Normalized Shannon Entropy (Hnorm) & Gini: Metric of distributional inequality | 5. Peak Timing Stability: Kendall's W rank concordance across 4 baseline years
key_visual: Metric Formulation Equations & Interpretive Threshold Reference Table
speaker_message: To evaluate seasonality without bias, we developed a multi-metric quantitative framework. We combined Seasonal Indices, Top-3 Concentration Ratios, Coefficient of Variation, and Gini inequality with non-parametric Kendall's W rank concordance across years.

slide_title: Seasonal Profiles of Primary Disease Families
purpose: Detail the core monthly distribution findings for each disease
on_slide_content: Dengue: June-October surge (82.8% of events); peak in Oct (19.6%, Sm=235.3) & Sep (17.6%, Sm=211.8) | Malaria: Contiguous May-July window (51.4% of events); peak in Jun (21.4%, Sm=257.1) & Jul (20.0%, Sm=240.0) | Acute Diarrheal Disease: Core monsoon elevation in Jun-Aug (43.1% of events; Jul peak 14.4%) + Oct surge (16.3%) | Food Poisoning: Bimodal calendar-month concentration in late winter (Jan-Feb, 26.1%) and spring (Apr-May, 29.0%) | Chikungunya: Diffuse distribution across year (May 14.0%, Jun 14.0%, Mar 11.6%, Sep 11.6%, Nov 11.6%)
speaker_message: Examining seasonal indices reveals distinct epidemiological profiles. Dengue is concentrated in the late monsoon and post-monsoon (June-October: 82.8%). Malaria peaks sharply in the early monsoon (May-July: 51.4%). Diarrheal diseases peak during mid-monsoon, while Food Poisoning displays bimodal winter and spring peaks.

purpose: Compare concentration levels across all 5 disease families
on_slide_content: High Concentration: Malaria (CV=0.753, CR3=51.4%, Gini=0.395) & Dengue (CV=0.736, CR3=50.5%, Gini=0.414) | Moderate Concentration: Food Poisoning (CV=0.564, CR3=44.9%) & Acute Diarrheal Disease (CV=0.524, CR3=43.1%) | Diffuse / Low Concentration: Chikungunya (CV=0.515, CR3=39.5%, Gini=0.289) | Key Insight: Vector-borne disease reports exhibit significantly tighter seasonal concentration than water-borne or food-borne outbreaks
speaker_message: Comparative concentration analysis groups our diseases into three distinct categories: Dengue and Malaria exhibit high seasonal concentration; Diarrheal Disease and Food Poisoning show moderate concentration; whereas Chikungunya exhibits diffuse baseline activity.

purpose: Examine whether seasonal patterns repeat consistently across years
on_slide_content: Acute Diarrheal Disease: Statistically significant rank concordance across years (Kendall's W=0.530, p=0.016, FDR-significant); 3 of 4 years show elevated Jun-Aug | Dengue: Moderate concordance (W=0.405, p=0.086, non-significant); peak month oscillates within 5-month window (Sep 2022, Oct 2023, Jun/Jul 2024, Aug 2025) | Food Poisoning: Moderate concordance (W=0.386, p=0.108, non-significant); timing shifts between winter and spring periods | Malaria: Timing window is fixed (May-Jul), but low non-parametric concordance (W=0.319, p=0.229, non-significant) due to small annual counts | Chikungunya: Unstable (W=0.150, p=0.832, non-significant); sparse records (7 events in 3 of 4 years)
speaker_message: Evaluating inter-annual stability via Kendall's W shows that Acute Diarrheal Disease exhibits the most reproducible monthly rank pattern across years (W=0.530, p=0.016). Dengue displays moderate stability (W=0.405, p=0.086), with peak months oscillating within a 5-month window. Chikungunya is unstable.

purpose: Analyze spatial heterogeneity and focalization across Maharashtra
on_slide_content: Malaria: Extreme geographic concentration; 2 forested districts (Gadchiroli: 27 events, 38.6%; Chandrapur: 16 events, 22.9%) account for 61.4% of statewide events | Chikungunya: Urban reporting concentration; Pune accounts for 25.6% of baseline events (11/43) | Dengue: Broad statewide reporting across 31 of 36 districts; 8 districts with >= 10 records (Thane, Beed, Raigad, Kolhapur, Nanded, Aurangabad, Akola, Pune) | Acute Diarrheal Disease: Broad statewide reporting across 33 districts; Nagpur, Amravati, Kolhapur qualify with >= 10 records
key_visual: Choropleth/Bar Chart: District Outbreak Event Concentration by Disease Family
speaker_message: Geographic analysis reveals crucial spatial heterogeneity. Malaria's statewide seasonal profile is heavily driven by just two eastern Vidarbha districts—Gadchiroli and Chandrapur—which account for 61.4% of events. In contrast, Dengue and ADD display broad statewide presence across over 30 districts.

purpose: Evaluate 2026 YTD surveillance records (W01-W32) without invalid forecasting
on_slide_content: Data Scope: 45 total primary records in 2026 W01-W32 (Historical equivalent mean = 75.8 events) | Acute Diarrheal Disease: 18 events vs 21.8 historical mean (-17.2%); expected seasonal baseline consistency | Food Poisoning: 19 events vs 12.8 historical mean (+49.0%); elevated early-year reporting; all 19 used 'Suspected' label | Dengue: 6 events vs 22.8 historical mean (-73.6%); severe truncation caveat as 55.4% of Dengue events occur in W33-W52 | Malaria: 1 event vs 12.0 historical mean (-91.7%); marked surveillance deficit in Gadchiroli | Rule: 2026 is partial-year (32 weeks); cannot be compared to full-year totals or used to forecast W33-W52
speaker_message: Using 2026 Weeks 01-32 as an out-of-sample comparison validates our model boundaries. Acute Diarrheal Disease closely matched historical early-year expectations. Dengue appears depressed, but this is an expected artifact of seasonal truncation, since over 55% of Dengue outbreaks occur after Week 32.

purpose: Demonstrate how high-case outbreak records distort aggregate metrics
on_slide_content: The Phenomenon: Outbreak event frequency and reported case volume diverge drastically in administrative data | ADD Divergence: February ranks #8 in events (5.9%) but #1 in cases (17.5%, 1,582 cases) due to a single 1,000-case institutional outbreak in Nanded (MAHA-2024-W06-001) | Food Poisoning Divergence: February accounts for 15.9% of events but 36.5% of cases; driven by 3 high-case outbreak records (Kolhapur 651, Parbhani 629, Solapur 335 = 1,615 cases), an extreme outlier effect | Malaria Divergence: December case peak (21.0%) driven by one 385-case cluster in Gadchiroli | Dengue Resilience: Balanced (Event CR3=50.5%, Case CR3=49.9%); no single record dominates
speaker_message: A vital data science insight is the divergence between outbreak events and case counts. In Diarrheal Disease and Food Poisoning, isolated high-case outbreak records generated thousands of cases, creating artificial case peaks in February. Excluding these outliers restores alignment between cases and events.

purpose: Explicitly articulate what the data can and cannot prove
on_slide_content: 1. Surveillance Threshold Bias: Captures investigated outbreak clusters meeting notification thresholds, NOT total population incidence or endemic disease burden | 2. Government Archive Gaps: 2023 missing Weeks 15, 51, 52 in official publications (Week 50 is present) | 3. Reporting Asymmetries: Single high-surveillance years dominate (Dengue 2023 = 51.0% of events; ADD 2024 = 46.4%) | 4. No Meteorological Confounding Control: Seasonality inferred from calendar months; climatic variables (rainfall, humidity, temperature) were not co-modeled | 5. Outlier Sensitivity: Case aggregates vulnerable to mass-exposure institutional records
key_visual: Boundary Matrix: Supported Surveillance Findings vs Unsupported Causal Claims
speaker_message: Academic integrity demands transparent limitations. Our dataset captures administrative outbreak investigations, not total community infections. We do not claim to measure true incidence, biological transmission rates, or direct climatic causation without meteorological data.

purpose: Present evidence-grounded takeaways and public health recommendations
on_slide_content: Conclusion 1 (Vector-Borne Concentration): Dengue (late-monsoon) and Malaria (early-monsoon) exhibit observable seasonal concentration in surveillance records | Conclusion 2 (Enteric Concentration): ADD displays consistent mid-monsoon elevation (Jun-Aug), but total cases depend on isolated contamination events | Conclusion 3 (Non-Climatic Point Sources): Food Poisoning reflects temporal cluster notifications in winter and spring rather than continuous weather cycles | Recommendation 1 (Pre-Monsoon): Pre-position Malaria diagnostics and vector spraying in Gadchiroli/Chandrapur by April-May | Recommendation 2 (Post-Monsoon): Intensify Dengue source reduction and hospital fever beds across Western Maharashtra by August-September
key_visual: Action Matrix: Surveillance Preparedness Windows by Disease Family
speaker_message: Our defensible conclusions prove distinct operational windows: Pre-position Malaria supplies in eastern Vidarbha by April; mobilize municipal Dengue vector squads across western Maharashtra by August; and fortify water testing for Diarrheal outbreaks during June-August.
